blogs.title: The Commissioner's Exclusive Domain: Parsing Private Rights to Penalties Under the MPWA
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's statutory interpretation of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA). It focuses on the court's distinction between an employee's right to recover unpaid wages versus the Commissioner's exclusive authority to assess 'average daily wage penalties.' The analysis will explore how the court utilized the 'knows how' canon of construction—comparing § 181.101 to other Minnesota statutes that explicitly grant private penalty rights—to conclude that the legislature intentionally reserved punitive enforcement for the state, limiting private plaintiffs to compensatory relief.

blogs.title: Voluntary Cessation and the Mootness Trap: When Full Payment Isn't Enough to Kill a Case
blogs.description: Focusing on the MFLSA claim, this entry examines the tension between a defendant's voluntary payment of all owed wages/liquidated damages and the potential survival of a claim for civil penalties. The post will dissect the Eighth Circuit's application of *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw*, highlighting why paying the plaintiff does not automatically moot a case when statutory penalties payable to the government remain at issue. It will discuss the remand instruction requiring the district court to determine if the employer's unlawful policy is still in effect, illustrating the high bar defendants face in proving that wrongful conduct cannot 'reasonably be expected to recur.'

blogs.title: Procedural Peril: Waiver, New Claims, and the Limits of Summary Judgment Briefing
blogs.description: This post addresses the procedural missteps that led to the dismissal of Cohen's MWTA notice claim and his request for injunctive relief. It serves as a cautionary tale for practitioners regarding Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a) and appellate waiver doctrines. The analysis will detail how attempting to introduce new theories of liability or altered requests for injunctive relief solely within opposition briefs—rather than through amended pleadings or proper pre-trial motions—can result in immediate forfeiture, regardless of the underlying merit of the statutory violation.
